'''Roland Kupers''' is a Dutch theoretical physicist, academic, and author. He is a [[consultant]] with work focused in [[complexity]], [[robustness|resilience]], and the [[energy transition]], as well as a professor of Practice at [[Arizona State University]].<ref name=aes>{{Cite web|url=https://search.asu.edu/profile/3636417|title=Roland Kupers &#124; ASU Search|website=search.asu.edu}}</ref>

Kupers has written on complexity, resilience, energy transition, and [[climate change]], examining their interdependencies to address challenges and develop policy approaches. His scholarly contributions include journal articles, book chapters, and books including ''The Essence of Scenarios: Learning from the Shell Experience'' and ''Complexity and the Art of Public Policy: Solving Society's Problems from the Bottom Up''. Additionally, his work has appeared in publications including the ''[[Harvard Business Review]]'' and ''[[Project Syndicate]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.project-syndicate.org/columnist/roland-kupers|title=Roland Kupers|website=Project Syndicate}}</ref> He contributed to a report commissioned by the German government on a new growth path for Europe.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/content/documents/1595TheNewClimateEconomyReport.pdf|title=Better Growth-Better Climate}}</ref>

Kupers serves as the Global Senior Advisor and Chief Architect of [[United Nations Environment Programme|UNEP's]] [[International Methane Emissions Observatory]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://2celsius.org/en/uneps-roland-kupers-a-methane-partnership-for-mitigating-climate-change/|title=Conference. UNEP's Roland Kupers: a methane partnership for mitigating climate change|first=Raul|last=Cazan|date=May 23, 2022}}</ref> and is a member of the Europe Advisory Council at the [[Environmental Defense Fund]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.edfeurope.org/environmental-defense-fund-europe-boards|title=Environmental Defense Fund Europe Boards &#124; Environmental Defense Fund|website=www.edfeurope.org}}</ref> He has served as an Advisor to the [[World Resources Institute]] and the [[Rockefeller Foundation]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.adipec.com/speaker-root/finance-investment-conference/dr-roland-kupers/|title=Dr. Roland Kupers|website=ADIPEC}}</ref> and, as a recipient of the Rockefeller Foundation Bellagio Residency, he contributed to discussions on climate solutions, [[economic transformation]], and well-being.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.rockefellerfoundation.org/news/rockefeller-foundation-bellagio-center-announces-2024-residents-opens-call-for-2025/#:~:text=2024+Bellagio+Center+Residents+(as,Foundation's+programmatic+work+and+priorities.|title=Rockefeller Foundation Bellagio Center Announces 2024 Residents; Opens Call for 2025}}</ref>

==Education and career==
Kupers completed his [[bachelor's degree]] in Physics and Philosophy in 1982, his [[master's degree]] in Theoretical Physics and Computer Science in 1988 from the State [[University of Groningen]] and a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] from [[Nyenrode Business University]] in 2014. After working at AT&T for over a decade, in 1998 he conducted research on organizational dynamics and published on [[complex system]]s. Between 1999 and 2009, he held various roles at Royal Dutch Shell, while also serving as a Senior Lecturer in Strategy at Nyenrode University from 2003 to 2019. In 2010, he became a Guest Researcher at the [[Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research]] and an [[Associate Professor]] in the Master of Public Affairs program at [[Sciences Po]], holding both positions until 2012. In 2010, he also took up the role of Associate Fellow at the [[University of Oxford]]'s [[Smith School of Enterprise and the Environment]], which he retained until 2017.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cepr.org/about/people/roland-kupers|title=Roland Kupers|website=CEPR}}</ref>

For a year, Kupers held the position of Research Director at the THNK School of Leadership from 2012 to 2013. In 2013, he was appointed as a visiting professor at [[Singapore Management University]] and as Global Methane Policy Advisor at the Environmental Defense Fund, positions he held until 2018 and 2020, respectively. Additionally, between 2018 and 2022, he was a Visiting Researcher at the Institute for Advanced Study, [[University of Amsterdam]], and since 2020, he has been a professor of Practice at the [[Thunderbird School of Global Management]], Arizona State University.<ref name=aes/>

==Works==
Kupers' research spans areas of theoretical physics, including complexity, resilience, and energy transition. In 2013, he examined how [[plausibility]]-based scenario practices grapple with 21st-century challenges, emphasizing their role in strategic renewal, systemic risk anticipation, and large-scale transitions—particularly in navigating complex, uncertain environments.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wilkinson |first1=Angela |last2=Kupers |first2=Roland |last3=Mangalagiu |first3=Diana |title=How plausibility-based scenario practices are grappling with complexity to appreciate and address 21st century challenges |journal=Technological Forecasting and Social Change |date=May 2013 |volume=80 |issue=4 |pages=699–710 |doi=10.1016/j.techfore.2012.10.031 }}{{primary source inline|date=March 2025}}</ref> In the following year, he edited ''Turbulence: A Corporate Perspective on Collaborating for Resilience'', which explored how multinational corporations leveraged resources and collaboration to enhance global resilience in food, water, and energy amid climate change. Alongside Colander, he co-authored ''Complexity and the Art of Public Policy: Solving Society's Problems from the Bottom Up'', exploring complexity science's impact on policy, critiqued traditional economics, and promoted 'activist laissez-faire' strategies for innovation, [[social entrepreneurship]], and adaptive governance. David Sloan Wilson, in his review of Complexity and the Art of Public Policy, described it as a milestone in applying scientific knowledge to real-world problem-solving. He further asserted that if widely read and implemented, the book could drive a long-overdue [[paradigm shift]], ultimately making the world a better place.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.rolandkupers.com/wp/wp-content/uploads/2016/06/The-Evolution-Institute.pdf|title=A Book That Changes The Way We Think About The Economy And Government}}</ref>

In 2020, Kupers authored ''A Climate Policy Revolution: What the Science of Complexity Reveals About Saving Our Planet'', examining how complexity science can drive responses to climate challenges. In a discussion about his book with Martin Reeves, he stated, "the main thesis is that the longer we wait to deal with climate, the faster we need to act." He further emphasized that "specifically, our insight into complex systems will be helpful and certainly more helpful than economics."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bcghendersoninstitute.com/embracing-the-complexity-of-climate-change/|title=Embracing the Complexity of Climate Change|first=François|last=Candelon|date=June 24, 2020|website=BCG Henderson Institute}}</ref> Joel Terwilliger, in his review of this book, stated that "Roland Kupers' book is an important contribution to understanding the limitations of current top-down and market-based approaches." Moreover, he further added that, "Kupers injects a healthy dose of optimism into the debate."<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Terwilliger |first1=Joel |title=A climate policy revolution: what the science of complexity reveals about saving our planet: by Roland Kupers. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2020. $29.95/£23.95/€27.00 (hardback). ISBN 9780674972124. |journal=Environmental Politics |date=19 September 2022 |volume=31 |issue=6 |pages=1102–1104 |doi=10.1080/09644016.2022.2079213 }}</ref>
